title: The Invisible Fibres
focus: Mixed and inverted conditionals (had we…, were to…)

lines.text: Good morning. Today I want to talk about synthetic fibres, which are probably the least visible source of plastic pollution in our oceans.
Every time we wash a fleece jacket, thousands of tiny fibres come loose and travel down the drain. Treatment plants catch many of them, but by no means all.
Had these fibres been easy to see, we would have regulated them decades ago. Because they're invisible, the problem has been largely ignored.
If a filter had been fitted as standard in every washing machine ten years ago, we would be seeing far fewer fibres in rivers today.
Now, I should be careful here. Finding fibres in a fish doesn't prove that they harm the fish, still less that they harm us.
What the evidence does show is that these particles are present almost everywhere researchers have looked, from mountain lakes to deep sediments.
Some manufacturers argue that consumers should simply wash their clothes less often. That's sensible advice, but it shifts the responsibility away from the industry.
A more convincing approach would be to design fabrics that shed less. A few companies are already doing this, although they tend not to advertise it.
Why not? Well, if the shedding were reduced, the clothes might also feel different, and customers notice that sort of thing.
So we have a classic dilemma. Were the industry to act voluntarily, it would risk losing customers; were it forced to act, every competitor would be in the same position.
That's precisely why I'd argue for regulation rather than appeals to goodwill. Standards level the playing field.
I'm not suggesting that individuals have no role. Fitting a filter at home is cheap and, as far as we can tell, effective.
But I'd be doing you a disservice if I implied that laundry habits alone could solve this.
For next week, please read the two papers on wastewater sampling, and think about what a fair testing standard would look like. Thank you.

options: She dismisses it as completely useless
She regards it as the ideal solution

She worries it will upset customers
questions.explain_es: Actitud. Dice: 'That's sensible advice, but it shifts the responsibility away from the industry.'

questions.explain_es: Implicatura. 'The clothes might also feel different, and customers notice that sort of thing.'

options: To argue that fish eat only synthetic fibres
To suggest that filters are not worth using
To warn that presence does not prove harm
To show that fish are in serious danger
questions.explain_es: Propósito. 'Finding fibres in a fish doesn't prove that they harm the fish, still less that they harm us.'

questions.q: Why does she prefer regulation to voluntary action?
options: Acting alone would confuse the testing standards
Acting alone would put a company at a disadvantage
Acting alone would be illegal for most companies
Acting alone would cost more than regulation does
questions.explain_es: Matiz. 'Were the industry to act voluntarily, it would risk losing customers'; 'Standards level the playing field.'

questions.q: The lecturer believes the fibres would have been regulated earlier if they had been visible.
questions.explain_es: 'Had these fibres been easy to see, we would have regulated them decades ago.'

questions.explain_es: Dice: 'Fitting a filter at home is cheap and, as far as we can tell, effective.'

dictation: Standards level the playing field.
Finding fibres in a fish doesn't prove that they harm the fish, still less that they harm us.

title: The Office Question
focus: Concessive clauses (much as, albeit, however + adjective)

lines.text: Welcome to tonight's panel. Our question is whether companies should require staff to return to the office. Daniel, you run a software firm, so let's start with you.
Much as I value flexibility, I've come to the view that new employees learn faster when they sit near experienced colleagues. That's my experience, albeit from a small sample.
Ingrid, you manage a team that's fully remote. Does that ring true?
Partly. However well a junior person is trained online, they miss the small things, like overhearing how a senior colleague handles a difficult call.
That said, we've compensated by pairing every newcomer with a mentor for the first three months, and it has worked better than I expected.
I'd accept that, though a mentor costs time, and time is exactly what small firms lack.
So is this really about money, Daniel, rather than culture?
Not entirely. Office space is expensive, admittedly, but I'd happily pay for it if it produced better work. My doubt is whether it does.
Which brings us to productivity. Whatever the surveys say, most managers I speak to can't actually measure it, so they rely on seeing people at their desks.
That's a little unfair. Seeing people is a poor measure, I agree, but it's not a meaningless one.
Perhaps. Yet however long someone sits at a desk, it tells you nothing about the quality of their thinking.
Let me bring in another angle. Employees often say that flexibility matters more to them than salary. Is that plausible?
For some, certainly. Though I suspect it's easier to say when you're already comfortably paid.
That's a fair point. Several of our staff care less about the location than about control over their own schedule.
So a compromise might be a fixed core of shared days, with freedom for the rest?
It might. Rigid rules, however well meant, tend to be resented, so I'd rather agree the pattern with each team.
I'd go along with that, as long as the agreement is reviewed regularly and nobody feels it's been imposed.

Certain that no evidence is needed
questions.explain_es: Actitud. Dice 'albeit from a small sample', reconociendo el límite de su experiencia.

questions.explain_es: Implicatura. 'Most managers I speak to can't actually measure it, so they rely on seeing people at their desks.'

questions.explain_es: Dice: 'it has worked better than I expected'.

title: Cartons, Quotas and Conditions
focus: Conditional connectors (provided that, unless, on condition that, as long as)

lines.text: Thanks for making time, Kofi. I'll be direct: your quote for the recycled cartons is higher than we budgeted.
I understand, Marta. Recycled board has become more expensive, and I can't absorb the increase entirely.
I'm not asking you to absorb all of it. But we'd be ordering twice our usual volume, so I'd expect that to count for something.
It does. Provided that you commit to the larger order for a full year, I can offer a reduction on the unit price.
A year is a long commitment. What if our sales dip?
Then I'd suggest a minimum quarterly quantity rather than a fixed annual one. Unless you fall below it twice running, the price would hold.
That's more workable. And what happens if you're late with a delivery? Last season that cost us dearly.
Fair enough. I'm prepared to accept a penalty clause on condition that it's capped. Otherwise I'd be carrying all the risk myself.
Capped at what level? I'd want it to be meaningful.
Say, a tenth of the order value. Anything higher and I'd have to raise the price to cover it.
Hmm. I could live with that as long as the delay is measured from the date on the confirmation, not from when you dispatch.
Agreed. Now, on the printing, I'm afraid I can't move. The inks cost the same whatever quantity you order.
In that case, I'll go back to my director with the reduced unit price and the quarterly minimum. I can't promise she'll approve it.
I appreciate your being candid. If she says yes, I'd like the contract signed before the end of the month, otherwise I'll have to release the production slot to another client.
Understood. I'll send you her answer by Friday.

title: Should a Machine Mark the Essay?
focus: Negative inversion for emphasis (seldom, under no circumstances, only when, no sooner)

lines.text: Tonight's motion: that artificial intelligence should mark student essays. Professor Ruiz, you're in favour.
I am, though not unconditionally. Seldom does a teacher have the time to give detailed feedback on a hundred essays, and the result is that students get a grade and a few scribbled words.
I'd challenge that. Not only does feedback from a person carry judgement, it carries a relationship. A student knows their teacher has read the work.
Does that matter if the comments are actually better? At no point have I suggested replacing the teacher. I'm suggesting a first reader.
A first reader that doesn't understand what a student is trying to say, only what they have managed to say. Those are different things.
Professor, is that a fair criticism?
In part. Rarely does a system grasp irony or a risky argument. But rarely do tired humans either, at eleven at night, on the fortieth essay.
Which is a good argument for giving teachers more time, not for handing the task over. Only when teachers are properly resourced will feedback improve.
Resources are what we lack, so I'm describing the world as it is. Little did I expect to hear you defend the status quo.
I'm not defending it. I'm saying that no sooner is a shortcut introduced than it becomes the standard.
That's a worry about drift, then, rather than about the technology itself.
Exactly. Under no circumstances should a machine decide a final grade on its own, whatever its accuracy.
On that we agree, actually. Were it used only to flag essays for a human to read, I'd be satisfied.
So the gap between you is narrower than the motion suggests?
Narrower, yes, though I'd still say the burden of proof lies with those who prefer the current system.
And I'd say it lies with those who want to change it. We'll doubtless keep disagreeing.
Thank you both. A lively exchange, and we'll leave it there.

Unconditional support for the motion
Neutrality towards the motion
questions.explain_es: Actitud. 'I am, though not unconditionally.'

title: A Decade of Cycle Lanes

lines.text: Doctor Rahman, your city has set a target for the next decade. How confident are you?
Cautiously optimistic. By the time the plan is complete, we'll have built over a hundred kilometres of protected cycle lanes, provided the funding holds.
That's a lot of paint. Will people actually use them?
Experience elsewhere suggests so. When a separated lane opens, cycling in that street typically rises quickly, because people who were frightened of traffic suddenly feel safe.
Critics say drivers will be furious, though.
Some will be. In five years' time, I think many of those drivers will be cycling themselves, or at least will have stopped noticing the change.
That's a bold prediction.
It's less bold than it sounds. This time next year we'll be reviewing the first results, and by then we'll have collected a full year of traffic data.
What would count as failure?
If journey times for buses had lengthened noticeably by then, I'd call that a problem and we'd change the design.
And shops? Traders often fear losing parking.
They do, and I take that seriously. But studies of high streets that removed parking suggest that people on foot and on bikes tend to visit more often, even if they spend less per visit.
So no downside at all?
I didn't say that. There'll be a difficult year while the roadworks are going on, and some businesses will be struggling by the end of it unless we support them.
Will you still be in the job to see it through?
Ha. By then I'll probably have retired, but I'll be cycling past the finished lanes, I hope.

title: The Message You Didn't Send
focus: Wishes and regrets (I wish I had, if only, would rather)

lines.text: Welcome back to Second Thoughts. Today, loneliness, and I'll admit I've got a personal angle.
Go on, Sam. I suspect you're about to confess something.
When I moved cities for work, I told myself I'd keep in touch with everyone. I wish I'd been more honest about how hard that would be.
Most of us say it. If only keeping in touch were as easy as intending to.
Exactly. And what surprised me is that I wasn't alone because nobody liked me. I was alone because I assumed everyone was busy.
That's well documented, actually. People tend to underestimate how much others would welcome a message.
So why don't we send it?
Fear of seeming needy, mostly. I wish someone had told me at twenty that sending a clumsy message is better than sending none.
I'd add that it matters what you say. 'We should meet sometime' is the kind of phrase that closes a door while appearing to open it.
Right, it sounds warm, but it commits nobody. 'Are you free on Thursday?' is much harder to ignore.
Though to be fair, some people would rather you didn't. I can think of one friend who'd have preferred I'd left him alone.
Then he'd have said so, surely. Sam, are you suggesting that you shouldn't have called?
No, no. I'm saying I'd rather have asked than assumed. If I'd asked, I'd have known.
That's perhaps the lesson. Not that we should be braver, but that we should stop pretending we can read minds.
I'd settle for being slightly braver, honestly. Starting with a text to someone I haven't spoken to in two years.
Then do it now. I'll stop recording while you write it.
Ha. It's a deal.

Accepting a job in another city
Ending a friendship by mistake

title: When Coral Turns White
focus: Passive reporting structures (is thought to, are said to have)

lines.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Coral reefs cover only a tiny fraction of the sea floor, yet they are thought to support an extraordinary share of marine life.
Today I'll explain bleaching, which is often misunderstood. Bleached coral is not dead coral, at least not at first.
Corals live in partnership with tiny algae inside their tissue. The algae provide most of the coral's food and give it its colour.
When the water stays too warm for too long, the coral is believed to expel the algae. What remains is a pale skeleton showing through transparent tissue.
If temperatures fall in time, the algae can return and the coral can recover. If not, the coral starves.
Mass bleaching events are reported to have become more frequent since the nineteen-eighties.
Now, here's something that is often overlooked. Some reefs are said to have recovered within a decade, while others have shown little sign of recovery. Why the difference?
Local conditions seem to matter. Reefs that are not smothered by sediment or fertiliser runoff are considered likelier to bounce back.
That's encouraging in one respect, since local pollution is something that can be controlled by local decisions, even when global warming cannot.
However, I'd be misleading you if I suggested that this was enough. Water temperature is expected to keep rising, and no amount of local management will prevent that.
There have also been claims that certain corals can adapt to heat. These corals are known to host different strains of algae, and some of those strains tolerate heat better.
Researchers are reported to be experimenting with moving heat-tolerant coral to damaged reefs. It's a promising idea, but it's thought to be expensive and hard to scale.
I'd therefore put it this way. Restoration is worth pursuing, but it's no substitute for cutting emissions.
Please read the two review papers before next week, and be ready to discuss which kind of intervention you consider most realistic.

questions.explain_es: Actitud. 'Restoration is worth pursuing, but it's no substitute for cutting emissions.'

questions.explain_es: Implicatura. 'If temperatures fall in time, the algae can return and the coral can recover.'

To show that part of the problem can be tackled locally

To argue that reefs cannot recover
questions.explain_es: Propósito. 'Local pollution is something that can be controlled by local decisions.' Pero añade que no basta.

title: Opt-Out and Organ Donation
focus: Modals of obligation and speculation (ought to, might well, needn't, must)

lines.text: Tonight we're asking whether organ donation should be opt-out, meaning that everyone is presumed to be a donor unless they say otherwise. Doctor Mehta?
I'd say we ought to, and I can't see how anyone could object on practical grounds. Many people support donation but never get round to registering. An opt-out system must surely close that gap.

It might, but it mustn't be assumed that it will. In some countries with presumed consent, donation rates haven't risen as much as supporters predicted. Other factors, like the number of intensive care beds, seem to matter more.
That could well be true. But those factors aren't mutually exclusive. We should be doing both.
I take the point. My real concern is consent. Silence can't be taken as agreement, can it?
In law, we accept all sorts of defaults. People may opt out at any time, and it ought to be easy to do so.
Easy for whom? A person in distress can hardly be expected to fill in forms. I'd have thought that a family at the bedside shouldn't be made to feel that a decision has been taken for them.
Agreed, which is why in most systems the family is still consulted. They needn't make the decision, but they must be informed.
Carla, is that enough to reassure you?
Partly. It would have to be backed by a big public campaign, otherwise people might not realise that they've been enrolled.
No argument there. A system that surprises people would be bound to lose trust.
Let me ask about the risk. Could opt-out actually reduce donation if people resent it?
It could, and that's the worst case. Some people may well sign out of principle, simply because they dislike being told what to do.
Possibly, but I don't think we should let that hypothetical outweigh the lives we know are lost on waiting lists.
That's a strong note to end on. Thank you both.

title: Whose Name on the Stage?

lines.text: Thanks for coming in, Mr Lawson. We're delighted that your company is interested in sponsoring the festival.
Please, call me Greg. We are, though I should say we've got some reservations about the proposal.
I'd be glad to hear them.
Well, the logo placement. Having our name on the main stage is lovely, but we'd rather it weren't alongside the beer brand. It might not sit well with our image.
I see. I'm afraid the beer sponsor has the contract for the bars, but I wonder whether we could separate the two on the screens.
That would help. I'd also have thought a stronger digital presence was part of the package.
It could be. I'm not sure we can promise that at this price, to be honest. Our app has a modest audience.
Then perhaps the price is a little optimistic. We'd be looking at a smaller figure.
I'd be reluctant to go lower than we've quoted, I'm afraid, as our costs this year are up. What I could do is add a branded stage on the second day.
That's an interesting thought. I'm not entirely convinced, though. A branded stage costs us in production.
True. Would you be open to sharing those costs, say, if we handled the design?
I'd have to check, but I think we might be able to. I wouldn't want to commit today.
Of course. There's no pressure. Perhaps we could put the main points in writing and talk again early next week?
That sounds sensible. I'll be honest, I'm leaning towards yes, as long as the beer issue is resolved.
Then I'll make that my priority. Thank you, Greg.

title: Bees on the Rooftop

lines.text: Rosa, you keep hives on the roof of an office block. Which, I have to say, sounds slightly mad.
It does, and the neighbours who first heard about it thought so too. But the district, whose parks and balconies are surprisingly full of flowers, turns out to be ideal.
Why is a city better than the countryside?

Not better in every case. But in the countryside, where large fields of a single crop dominate, bees often have nothing to eat for weeks. A city offers a mixture of plants that flower at different times, which keeps the colony fed.
That's counterintuitive.
It is, which is partly why people are surprised by the honey. It tastes different from street to street, depending on the trees that are nearby.
How far do the bees travel?
Usually a few kilometres, though that depends on what's available. The bees on my rooftop, which are very efficient, don't need to go far.
So everyone should keep bees?
Here's where I'd disagree. The idea that every rooftop should have a hive is, frankly, a mistake, and it's one that conservationists have been warning about.
Why would that be a mistake?
Because honeybees, which are managed animals, compete with wild bees, many of which are in decline. If a city fills up with hives, the wild species, on which our flowers also depend, lose out.
So what would you recommend instead?
Plant more flowers, which costs very little, and leave a bit of bare soil for the solitary bees, most of which nest in the ground.
That's a surprisingly modest message from someone who loves beekeeping.
It's the honest one. The people I respect most in this field are those who'd happily give up their hives if the evidence required it.

questions.q: What is Rosa's attitude to the idea that everyone should keep bees?
options: Sceptical, because it may harm wild bees
Neutral, because of the costs
Enthusiastic, because of the honey
Alarmed, because of the neighbours
questions.explain_es: Actitud. 'The idea that every rooftop should have a hive is, frankly, a mistake.'

questions.q: What does Amir imply by calling her message 'surprisingly modest'?
options: He suspects her of hiding something
He wants a stronger message about honey
He expected her to promote beekeeping more
He doubts the evidence she cites
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. 'Surprisingly modest message from someone who loves beekeeping.'

questions.q: Why does Rosa mention the countryside?
options: To prove that honey tastes better there
To criticise country beekeepers
To suggest that bees travel far
To explain why cities can suit bees
questions.explain_es: Propósito. Allí dominan los grandes cultivos únicos, mientras la ciudad ofrece 'a mixture of plants that flower at different times'.

questions.q: What does she recommend instead of more hives?
options: Moving the hives out to farmland
Planting more flowers and leaving bare soil
Building bigger hives for each colony
Banning all sales of urban honey
questions.explain_es: 'Plant more flowers, which costs very little, and leave a bit of bare soil.'

questions.q: Rosa says bees in the countryside always have more food than city bees.
questions.explain_es: Dice que en el campo, con un solo cultivo, 'bees often have nothing to eat for weeks'.

questions.q: She says honey can taste different from one street to the next.
questions.explain_es: 'It tastes different from street to street.'

dictation: It tastes different from street to street, depending on the trees that are nearby.
Plant more flowers, which costs very little, and leave a bit of bare soil for the solitary bees.
